title: Buddy Petit's playing, repertoire and Kid Rene
summary: Petit played cornet by ear, drank hard, played Scott Joplin-type numbers, and rivalled Kid Rene, whose reputation rose above Armstrong's locally.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Well he must have been a fine cornet player, trumpet player.
Well he wasn't that exact, but I mean when he played, he played. Uh-huh.
Did he play trumpet or cornet then?

Yeah, played cornet. Was he a hard worker or did he? Oh he was a hard worker. He was a hard drinker too. Yeah, he, he, he. Where did he live then, those days when you played? Those days he was living on Durbanie, between St. Anthony and Poggle.
A guy like Buddy, would he play the whole tune or would he take down or what?

Well I tell you, the number that Buddy used to play with, lots of these trumpet players around here couldn't play. Now I don't know how he played. He used to play what we called Scott Joplin number. The Red Bulls, we called it the Red Bulls. But all things like that. And that's what you used to get, the people used to be crazy about what they kind of knew during that time.
Uh-huh. Did he, did he read those books or did he just have-
Well, not to mind knowing, he didn't read, but I know he got them. How you got them, he got them.
Well, did anybody in the band, I mean, were any of those members that you mentioned, were they readers at all? Not that I know of.

Never used the arrangements then, never had the music there for any of those. They let him just play what they, what they thought went, did it sound good? And he had the biggest reputation around here, and then the trumpet player. And then another one had a big reputation around here, Kid René. Kid René had a bigger reputation than Louis Armstrong. Just say he didn't want to go away from him, he had the best opportunity of his life. They're begging him, come to Chicago. King Alba wanted to send him to him. He said to go. They used to call him the little Turk. And when we'd, uh, that time we used to advertise the truck, you know, like I said, for a dance going on, you might catch about three or four bands that's out on the streets, for different places giving dances. And when they tell you little Turk's at the next corner, they could be going that way, they wouldn't go that way, they'd go around the corner. It's like, like a dog, your friend, play the past, play the bulldog on by them. So, let's keep out the way. That was a kick. That was good days, those days.
